title: Martin de Porres (1579–1639)
hookLine: a mixed-race Dominican brother in Lima, with a broom, a clinic, and mice he fed

lines: NOT A BOOK, NOT A SWORD.
A DOG, A CAT, A MOUSE.
cards: Statues of him often show the same things: a Dominican in a black and white habit, a dark-skinned face, and in his hand, not a book or a sword, but a broom.
Sometimes a dog, a cat and a mouse eat from one bowl at his feet. It looks like a children's picture. It's actually a summary of a life.
He swept floors, cut hair, set bones, fed the hungry at the door, and for a long time held the lowest place in his house. Today, Martin de Porres.

teach.b: First, where he started. Martin was born in Lima, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Black woman. His father didn't acknowledge him at first.
The colonial world sorted people by race, and Martin landed near the bottom. Second, a door half open. He trained as a barber, which then also meant small surgery and setting bones.
Then he asked to join the Dominicans. The rules of the time kept men like him from full vows, so he entered as a donado, a lay helper who gave his work to the house. He swept.
He cleaned. Only later did the community admit him as a professed brother. Third, the clinic.
As infirmarian he cared for sick friars, and the care spread out the door: to slaves, to the city's poor, to anyone who came. Fourth, the stories.
Tradition says that when the priory was short of money, Martin offered to be sold to pay its debts. Tradition says he struck a deal with the house mice: stay in the garden, and I'll feed you there.
Some are legends, retold many times; even so, they point one way.
He took the lowest place and made it holy.
Jesus describes himself in that place, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am in the midst of you, as he that serveth."
It's the claim his life makes: sweeping a floor for God is not a lesser kind of prayer.

how: Catholics often show Saint Martin de Porres with a broom, and some parishes and schools named for him run food pantries or outreach to the poor; he is invoked by people who face racial prejudice.

o: a lay helper who gives his work to a house
a novice priest in his first year of study
a wealthy patron who funds a monastery

games.q: Martin de Porres — tap the pairs.
p: a lay helper who gave his work

s: Martin entered the Dominicans as a full brother from the start
the rules of the time kept him out of full vows. he entered as a donado, and was professed later.
Martin trained as a barber, which included setting bones
barbers then did small surgery too, and he became the house's infirmarian.
the broom in his statues is just decoration
it sums up his life: the lowest work, done for God.

games.q: you're Martin. the priory is short of money and in debt. what do you offer?
o: to beg in the streets for a week.
to be sold, to pay the debt.
to leave so there's one less mouth to feed.
games.why: tradition says he offered himself to be sold. the community did not take him up on it.

practice: Think of one small chore waiting for you, the kind nobody thanks anyone for, and picture doing it slowly, without hurrying to be done. If a voice says this is beneath me, let it speak and pass.
If you pray, offer the chore to God before you start; if not, simply decide to do it well.

wordCard.voice: Donado. A lay helper who gives his work to the house without taking full vows, the place Martin de Porres entered before the community made him a professed brother.

carryVoice: Your line: the saint with a broom. In Martin's hands, the lowest place became holy. That's day eight hundred fifty-nine.
